Maximisation bias

Q-learning's target takes the max over estimated action values. When the estimates are noisy, the largest one is usually one that got lucky, so the max is biased upwards. Double Q-learning removes the bias by choosing the action with one estimate and scoring it with another.

The max of noisy zeros

Every arm has true value 0. Each estimate is an average of noisy rewards $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$. The single estimate takes the largest average. The double estimate splits each arm's rewards into two halves, picks the arm with the best first half (purple outline), and reports that arm's second half.

S&B Example 6.7

From A, going left leads to B and then to a reward with mean $-0.1$, so left is worse than right ($0$). But B's 10 actions each have noisy estimates, and Q-learning's $\max_a Q(\text{B}, a)$ is usually positive early on, which makes left look good. ε-greedy with $\varepsilon = 0.1$, $\alpha = 0.1$, $\gamma = 1$.

Percentage of runs that went left from A, out of 1,000 runs per method. The best possible under ε-greedy is 5%: exploration picks left with probability $\varepsilon/2$.

The maths

Let $Q(a)$ be unbiased estimates of true values $q(a)$, so $\mathbb{E}[Q(a)] = q(a)$. For any fixed action $b$, $\max_a Q(a) \ge Q(b)$. Take expectations:

$$\mathbb{E}\big[\max_a Q(a)\big] \ge \mathbb{E}[Q(b)] = q(b) \ \text{ for every } b, \quad\text{so}\quad \mathbb{E}\big[\max_a Q(a)\big] \ge \max_a q(a)$$

The max of estimates overestimates the max of true values. Equality needs the estimate of the truly best action to come out on top every time, which noise almost never allows. For two estimates that are independent $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, $\mathbb{E}[\max] = 1/\sqrt{\pi} \approx 0.56$ even though both true values are 0.

The fix is to use independent estimates for the two jobs: choosing and scoring. With independent $Q_1, Q_2$:

$$A^* = \arg\max_a Q_1(a), \qquad \mathbb{E}\big[Q_2(A^*) \mid A^*\big] = q(A^*) \le \max_a q(a)$$

$Q_2$'s noise had no say in picking $A^*$, so it is unbiased for the chosen action. It can underestimate (if $Q_1$ picks a worse action) but never systematically overestimates.

Double Q-learning keeps two tables. Each step, with probability ½, it updates $Q_1$ with

$$Q_1(S_t, A_t) \leftarrow Q_1(S_t, A_t) + \alpha\Big[R_{t+1} + \gamma\, Q_2\big(S_{t+1}, \arg\max_a Q_1(S_{t+1}, a)\big) - Q_1(S_t, A_t)\Big]$$

and otherwise does the same with $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ swapped. Each experience updates only one table, so the two stay independent estimates. Actions are chosen ε-greedily on $Q_1 + Q_2$. The memory doubles, the computation per step does not.
